name: Ahaz
title: King of Judah and ancestor of Jesus
summary: Ahaz, known by the Hebrew name form Akas (Ahaz), was king over the kingdom of Judah and is listed in Matthew's genealogy as an ancestor in the messianic line from David to Jesus Christ. As son of King Jotham and father of the godly King Hezekiah, he reigned for sixteen years, from about 735 to 715 BC. Despite his place in the Davidic royal line, Ahaz stands out as one of Judah's most faithless kings. He introduced widespread idolatry, had his son pass through the fire as an offering to foreign gods, and altered the temple's sacred furnishings according to pagan patterns. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, when Aram and the northern kingdom of Israel threatened Jerusalem, he sought military support from Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III rather than trusting in the Lord's promises delivered through the prophet Isaiah. It was in this tense situation that Isaiah proclaimed the famous sign of Immanuel. Ahaz's reign led Judah into political vassalage under Assyria and represented a profound spiritual decline. According to Chronicles, Judah also suffered serious military defeats as a result of the king's unfaithfulness. Nevertheless, God's faithfulness to the Davidic covenant was shown by the fact that the messianic line continued through his son Hezekiah, who carried out sweeping religious reforms and restored the worship of the Lord.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in Jesus' genealogy
keyEvents.description: Ahaz is listed as a link in Jesus' lineage from Abraham through David and the royal line of Judah, between his father Jotham and his son Hezekiah.

keyEvents.title: Became king over Judah
keyEvents.description: Ahaz became king of Judah at twenty years old and reigned for sixteen years in Jerusalem. Unlike his father Jotham and his ancestor David, he did not walk uprightly in the Lord's sight.

keyEvents.title: Idolatry and child sacrifice
keyEvents.description: Ahaz followed the customs of the Canaanite peoples, sacrificed on the high places, and made his son pass through the fire – an abominable practice that the Lord had condemned.

keyEvents.title: The Syro-Ephraimite War
keyEvents.description: Aram's king Rezin and Israel's king Pekah formed a coalition against Judah and threatened Jerusalem. The prophet Isaiah met Ahaz with a message to hold fast to faith in the Lord amid the crisis.

keyEvents.title: The Sign of Immanuel
keyEvents.description: When Ahaz refused to ask the Lord for a sign, the prophet Isaiah still gave the sign of Immanuel: that a young woman would conceive and bear a son named Immanuel ('God with us'). This prophecy was understood in Christian tradition as fulfilled at Jesus' birth.

keyEvents.title: Alliance with Assyria
keyEvents.description: Instead of trusting in God, Ahaz sent word to Tiglath-Pileser III, king of Assyria, asking for military help. He sent silver and gold from the temple and the royal treasury as tribute, thereby making Judah a vassal state.

keyEvents.title: Judah's Military Defeat
keyEvents.description: During Ahaz's reign, Judah suffered serious military losses against several enemies, including Aram, the northern kingdom of Israel, the Philistines, and the Edomites. The Chronicler presents this as direct consequences of the king's unfaithfulness to the Lord.

keyEvents.title: Changes in the Temple
keyEvents.description: After seeing a pagan altar in Damascus, Ahaz had a similar altar built in the Lord's temple in Jerusalem and altered the temple's original furnishings to please the king of Assyria.

keyEvents.title: The Death of Ahaz
keyEvents.description: Ahaz died and was buried, but according to the Books of Chronicles he was not laid among the graves of Israel's kings. His son Hezekiah succeeded him and carried out extensive religious reforms.

versions.summary: Ahaz (also known as Ahaz in other translations) is mentioned in Matthew's genealogy as one of Jesus' ancestors. He was the son of Jotham and father of Hezekiah, and reigned as king over Judah. His reign was marked by idol worship and political alliances with Assyria.
versions.title: Judas son in Jesus' genealogy
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Judas son in Jesus' genealogy' is misleading. Ahaz was not the son of Judah (the patriarch), but of Jotham, and was king over Judah (the kingdom). A more accurate title should reflect his role as king over Judah.; [minor] The phrasing '(also known as Ahaz in other translations)' implicitly refers to specific Bible versions. It should be rephrased more neutrally, e.g., 'also known as Akas/Ahaz'.; [minor] Ahaz was also an ancestor of Jesus in the genealogy. The role 'ancestor of Jesus' or similar could have been included for completeness.; [minor] According to 2 Chronicles 29:1, Hezekiah's mother was Abia, daughter of Zechariah. Ahaz's wife (Hezekiah's mother) can thus be identified as Abia/Abi (2 Kings 18:2). This could have been included as spouse.; [major] Footnotes are completely missing. The profile should include footnotes on, for example, the Syro-Ephraimite War, the Immanuel prophecy in Isaiah 7, the Hebrew name, and archaeological findings related to Ahaz.; [minor] The sign of Immanuel (Isa 7:10-16) is a very important event connected to Ahaz that is missing as a separate key event. Isaiah's prophecy about the virgin sign was given specifically to Ahaz.

versions.summary: Ahaz (also known as Ahas or Ahaz) is mentioned in Matthew's genealogy as one of Jesus' ancestors. He was the son of Jotham and father to Hezekiah, and reigned as king over Judah for sixteen years. His reign was marked by idolatry, including child sacrifice, and political alliances with Assyria rather than trust in God. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, he chose to seek Assyrian help instead of listening to the prophet Isaiah's message to trust in the Lord. It was in this context that Isaiah gave the famous sign of Immanuel. Ahaz's reign represents a low point in Judah's spiritual history, yet God preserved the Davidic line through his son Hezekiah.
versions.title: King of Judah and ancestor of Jesus
versions.reason: [minor] The lifespan 'ca. 735–715 BC' is somewhat imprecise. According to 2 Kgs 16:2, Ahaz became king at age twenty and reigned for sixteen years. Standard dating places his reign around 735–715 BC, but this would mean he was born around 755 BC. The lifespan should reflect the entire life, not just the period of kingship, even if the death date coincides with the end of his reign.; [minor] According to 2 Kgs 18:2 (and 2 Chr 29:1), Hezekiah's mother was named Abi (or Abijah). The value 'abi' is acceptable, but it may be worth noting that some sources use the form 'Abijah'. Nevertheless, the ID 'abi' remains consistent.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but it mainly uses the name 'Ahaz' instead of the profile name 'Akussat'. Since the profile is named Akussat, this name should be used more consistently, even though it is common to mention alternative name forms.; [minor] An event concerning Ahaz's death and burial (2 Kgs 16:19–20) is missing, which marks the end of his reign and the transition to Hezekiah.

versions.summary: Ahaz, also known by the Hebrew name form Akas (Ahaz), is a central figure in the history of Judah's kings and is mentioned in Matthew's genealogy as an ancestor of Jesus Christ. He was the son of King Jotham and father of the godly King Hezekiah, and he reigned over Judah for sixteen years from about 735 to 715 BC. Despite his place in the Davidic line, Ahaz is known as one of Judah's most unfaithful kings. He introduced widespread idolatry, had his son pass through the fire as an offering, and replaced the temple's sacred furnishings with foreign cult objects. During the Syro-Ephraimite war, when Aram and the northern kingdom of Israel threatened Jerusalem, he chose to ally himself with Assyria's king Tiglath-Pileser instead of trusting in the Lord's promises delivered through the prophet Isaiah. It was in this dramatic situation that Isaiah proclaimed the famous sign of Immanuel. Ahaz's reign represents a spiritual low point in Judah's history, but God's faithfulness to the Davidic covenant was shown as the messianic line continued through his son Hezekiah, who carried out extensive religious reforms.
versions.title: King of Judah and ancestor of Jesus
versions.reason: [minor] The spouse 'Abi' is correct based on 2 Kings 18:2, where Hezekiah's mother is called Abi (daughter of Zechariah). In 2 Chronicles 29:1 she is called Abijah. This is acceptable, but it may be worth noting the variation.; [major] The Greek form in Matthew 1:9 is Ἀχάζ (Achaz), not 'Akussat'. It is unclear where the form 'Akussat' originates from. The footnote's claim that "the Greek form Akussat is used in Matthew's genealogy" is misleading – standard Greek manuscripts have Ἀχάζ.; [minor] The summary is well written and theologically balanced. A small improvement could be made by clarifying that 2 Chronicles provides further details about his decline, to give a more complete picture.; [minor] An event concerning Judah's military defeat under Ahaz's rule as described in 2 Chronicles 28 could have been included, since this complements the picture of the consequences of his unfaithfulness.

footnotes.text: The name Akussat reflects the Greek form Ἀχάζ (Achaz) from Matthew's genealogy. The underlying Hebrew name is אָחָז (Ahaz), likely a short form of Jehoahaz (יְהוֹאָחָז), meaning 'the Lord has grasped.' The short form Ahaz simply means 'he has grasped/held fast.'

The Syro-Ephraimite War (c. 735–732 BC) arose when Aram (Syria) under King Rezin and the northern kingdom of Israel under King Pekah attempted to force Judah into an anti-Assyrian coalition. Ahaz chose to seek help from Assyria's Tiglath-Pileser III, making Judah a vassal state with far-reaching political and religious consequences for the kingdom.

In connection with the Syro-Ephraimite crisis, the prophet Isaiah gave the famous sign of Immanuel (Isa 7:14). The prophecy had an immediate historical context linked to the contemporary crisis but was later in Christian tradition understood as a messianic prophecy fulfilled at Jesus' birth (cf. Matt 1:23). The Hebrew word 'almah' (young woman) was rendered in the Greek Septuagint with 'parthenos' (virgin), which had great significance for the Christian interpretation.

Assyrian annals from Tiglath-Pileser III mention a 'Jehoahaz of Judah' (Ia-ú-ha-zi) who paid tribute, confirming the biblical account of Ahaz's vassalage to Assyria. In addition, a seal impression with the text 'belonging to Ahaz (son of) Jotham, king of Judah' has been found, regarded as an important archaeological witness to this king.

Rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Sanhedrin 103b) counts Ahaz among the kings who have no share in the world to come, due to his extensive idolatry and alleged closing of Torah study places. Nevertheless, his son Hezekiah was counted among Judah's most godly kings—a contrast that rabbis reflected upon as an example that a righteous son can come from an ungodly father.

According to 2 Chronicles 28, Judah suffered great military losses during Ahaz's reign, with defeats against Aram, Israel, the Philistines, and the Edomites. The Chronicler gives an even more negative portrayal than the Books of Kings and emphasizes that Ahaz's troubles were direct consequences of his unfaithfulness to the Lord, including the loss of 120,000 soldiers in a single day.
